patient.chief_complaint: Acute confusion and unusual behavior — psychiatric vs metabolic
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. W. is a 52-year-old woman with bipolar disorder type I and unacknowledged alcoholic cirrhosis who was brought to the ED by her sister for acute confusion and 'weird behavior' over the prior 24 hours. Her sister describes pressured speech, disorganized thinking, limited sleep, and running out of her apartment to 'check on the neighbors' repeatedly — behaviors that appear similar to prior manic episodes. The patient was last psychiatrically hospitalized 2 years ago for a manic episode. She is adherent with her medications per sister. However, on careful review: valproate is HEPATOTOXIC and can cause hyperammonemia independent of liver disease (valproate inhibits urea cycle); valproate also can cause hepatitis in patients with pre-existing liver disease. Her ammonia is 76 µmol/L — moderately elevated. Her valproate level is 118 µg/mL — supratherapeutic (therapeutic 50-100 µg/mL). The diagnostic puzzle: (1) psychiatric presentation that looks manic; (2) valproate-induced hyperammonemia as a distinct cause (valproate inhibits urea cycle carbamyl phosphate synthase); (3) concurrent alcoholic cirrhosis with HE; (4) lithium potentially toxic (pending level); (5) quetiapine CNS depression. The key insight: valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy EVEN IN PATIENTS WITHOUT LIVER DISEASE — in this cirrhotic patient, the ammonia-raising effect of valproate is amplified.

results.title: Mood stabilizer selection in hepatic impairment
results.summary: Valproate is contraindicated or should be used with extreme caution in hepatic impairment — causes dose-dependent hyperammonemia via urea cycle inhibition and is hepatotoxic. Lithium is renally eliminated and safe in liver disease but requires careful monitoring (thiazide diuretics increase levels). Lamotrigine is the preferred alternative mood stabilizer in hepatic impairment — primarily renally eliminated, no hepatotoxicity. Lamotrigine requires slow titration to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

output.summary: In patients with hepatic impairment, valproate is associated with dose-dependent hyperammonemia via urea cycle inhibition and carries hepatotoxic risk; published case series and pharmacokinetic studies support cautious use or avoidance. Lithium is renally eliminated and its clearance is reduced by thiazide diuretics, a well-documented interaction associated with toxicity. Lamotrigine has a renal elimination pathway and lacks known hepatotoxic effects in the published literature.

critical_actions: HOLD VALPROATE — valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy is the primary precipitant; valproate inhibits urea cycle enzyme CPSI, raising ammonia even WITHOUT liver disease; in cirrhosis, this effect is amplified
STOP HCTZ — causing lithium toxicity via reduced renal clearance; a classic drug interaction

L-carnitine IV may help valproate-induced hyperammonemia acutely — valproate depletes carnitine which is required for mitochondrial function and ammonia metabolism

HCTZ continuation with lithium — lithium toxicity from thiazide interaction
Haloperidol for agitation — patient has documented allergy (dystonic reaction)

key_reasoning_points: Valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy (VIHE) — valproate inhibits CPS1 (urea cycle step 1), raising ammonia independent of liver disease; in cirrhosis, the effect is dramatically amplified; VIHE can occur without elevated transaminases or liver failure
HCTZ-lithium interaction — thiazide diuretics reduce renal lithium clearance by promoting sodium reabsorption (lithium follows sodium); toxicity risk is well-documented but frequently missed
Mania vs HE: pressured speech and agitation can mimic mania — the presence of asterixis, supratherapeutic drug levels, and elevated ammonia should redirect to metabolic etiology
Multiple simultaneous drug precipitants (valproate + lithium + ethanol + quetiapine) additive with cirrhotic HE baseline — addressing ALL precipitants is required for full recovery
